locator: I q.2 a.3 ad 1: ut esse permittat mala, et ex eis eliciat bona
interpretation: Reading B of the plural final sentence: the evils (mala, ex eis) are taken together, not distributed over every individual evil. Restricted to a nonempty collection that God permits, the reading says that he actually draws some good from that collection. The conclusion is existential over a bearer and a perfection; it assigns no good to each evil. Evil is the privative sense clarified in q.48 a.3, not automatically a moral judgment. PermitsEvils and DrawsGoodFromEvils are distinct parameters: permission alone does not entail production without this open reading. The sentence is stronger than mere capability on this actual-production interpretation. Neither the existence of God, evil or permission nor a net benefit, best world, benefit to every sufferer or justification of each evil is asserted. The coordinated permittat and eliciat are subjunctives under pertinet ut, not indicative event assertions: the conditional actual-production consequent is the policy construal of that coordination, preserved as a defensible interpretation rather than forced by the grammar. The capability sibling records a weaker extraction from the preceding clause.
